_meta.question: What does the field know in 2026 that this project is not using, that (a) runs on 8 CPU cores / 5 GB free, (b) is orthogonal to BLOSUM retrieval + the ESM distogram, (c) could rescue the 18 zero-recall targets?
_meta.box: 8 cores (6.4 fast-core equiv), 16 GB RAM (~5 GB free), no GPU, torch 2.13 CPU, OpenMM CPU
_meta.cpu_feasible_scale: YES = runs in <1 min/target in <1.2 GB; MARGINAL = minutes/target or 2-4 GB; NO = needs GPU or >5 GB
_meta.leakage_scale: NONE / LOW / HIGH  (HIGH = the model's training set almost certainly contains this benchmark's deposited structures)

methods.name: AlphaFold2 (monomer, ColabFold)
methods.predicts: single all-atom structure + pLDDT
methods.training_data_cutoff: PDB <= 2018-04-30 (train), CASP14 eval; ColabFold MSA from UniRef/env DBs
methods.short_length_performance: Structure 2023 benchmark, 588 NMR peptides 10-40 aa: mean RMSD/residue 0.098 (alpha-helical membrane, n=187), 0.119 (alpha-helical soluble, n=41), 0.146 (beta-hairpin, n=59), 0.068 (disulfide-rich, n=266), 0.202 (mixed membrane, n=14). NO correlation between AF2 rank/pLDDT and lowest-RMSD model. Separately: on 190 monomeric NMR structures AF2 failed on 128 (67.3%), AF3 on 135 (71%), ESMFold on 139 (73%) vs 95%/83% success on X-ray/cryoEM.
methods.code_weights: open (Apache-2.0 code, CC-BY-NC weights); ColabFold open
methods.cpu_feasible: NO for the full pipeline (MSA search + 93M-param Evoformer x 48 blocks x 3 recycles; ~10-30 min/target on CPU and >5 GB with templates). Also MSA depth for a 13-mer is effectively zero, which is the regime where AF2 has no advantage.
methods.leakage_risk: HIGH - most benchmark targets are pre-2018 PDB depositions inside the AF2 training set
methods.orthogonality: Weak in principle: AF2 without an MSA degenerates to a single-sequence PLM-free predictor. Its documented peptide failure modes (phi/psi recovery, kinks/turns, extended flexible regions, no pLDDT-RMSD correlation) are the SAME failure modes as this pipeline. Not an orthogonal channel.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Not recommended as a component. Useful only as a published reference point: the field's flagship also fails on ~70% of monomeric NMR structures, which sets a realistic expectation for this benchmark.

methods.name: AlphaFold3 / Boltz-1 / Boltz-2 / Chai-1 / Protenix
methods.predicts: all-atom complexes (diffusion decoder), confidence + affinity (Boltz-2)
methods.training_data_cutoff: PDB <= 2021-09-30 for both AF3 and Boltz-1; AF3's validation window 2021-09-30..2023-01-13 was used for model selection (documented leakage into 'post-cutoff' evaluations)
methods.short_length_performance: Benchmarks are protein-PEPTIDE COMPLEX benchmarks (PepPCBench, PepBDB-derived), not isolated peptides: Fnat >= 0.8 counted as high accuracy. Cyclic peptide-protein: median top-pose DockQ ~0.89 over 111 complexes, but disulfide-cyclised peptides and small targets significantly worse. On monomeric NMR structures AF3 fails 71%. On lasso peptides AF3 fails 10/12 (83%) on a PDB set and reaches 8% success on the harder RODEO set.
methods.code_weights: Boltz-1/2 MIT (code+weights); Chai-1 open weights non-commercial; AF3 weights request-only; Protenix open
methods.cpu_feasible: NO. Diffusion trunk + 100 poses; authors run H100s. Even a 13-mer needs the full pairformer stack and an MSA/template pipeline.
methods.leakage_risk: HIGH (pre-2021 targets); MEDIUM for 8T63/9KAR/9L1M (2023-2025)
methods.orthogonality: The relevant literature is all COMPLEX prediction; the isolated-peptide monomer case is nearly unstudied and is where all of these fail. No orthogonal channel obtainable on this box.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: None. Record as evidence that the benchmark's task (isolated 9-16-mer NMR peptides) is an acknowledged blind spot of the whole AF3-like family.

methods.name: ESMFold
methods.predicts: single structure from single sequence via ESM-2 3B + folding trunk
methods.training_data_cutoff: ESM-2 on UniRef50 (2021 snapshot); folding head on PDB <= 2020-05
methods.short_length_performance: CASP14 mean lDDT 0.68 (vs AF2 0.85); CAMEO TM 0.90/0.79/0.45 (easy/med/hard); median RMSD 1.74 A over 1,337 PDB chains (vs AF2 1.30, OmegaFold 1.98). Fails 139/190 (73%) monomeric NMR structures. Only 2.8% of UniRef50 is <50 residues, so short peptides are severely underrepresented in the PLM training distribution.
methods.source_of_number: Science 2023; NAR Genomics Bioinf 2026 lqag002; PMC12844563
methods.code_weights: open, MIT (fair-esm)
methods.cpu_feasible: NO as shipped: esmfold_v1 uses ESM-2 3B (~11 GB fp32 / 5.6 GB fp16) + a 48-block folding trunk. Exceeds the 5 GB budget. The 650M ESM-2 already on disk is the LM only, not a folding trunk.
methods.leakage_risk: HIGH for pre-2020 targets
methods.orthogonality: Its errors are PLM-attention errors - the same source as the project's ESM-2 distogram features. Low orthogonality by construction.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Not feasible and not orthogonal. Do not pursue.

methods.name: SimpleFold (Apple)
methods.predicts: all-atom backbone via flow matching, plain transformer (no triangle updates)
methods.training_data_cutoff: PDB + ~8.6-9M distilled AFDB/AFESM structures; PDB filter lists published in repo
methods.short_length_performance: No peptide-specific numbers published; benchmarked on CAMEO22/CASP14 monomers.
methods.code_weights: code MIT; weights under a separate LICENSE_MODEL; sizes 100M/360M/700M/1.1B/1.6B/3B released
methods.cpu_feasible: MARGINAL. The 100M checkpoint on a 13-token sequence is ~2.6 GFLOP/forward; 500 flow steps is ~1.3 TFLOP ~= 1 min on 2 cores. BUT it conditions on ESM-2 embeddings, and the required ESM-2 size must be confirmed - if it is 3B the pipeline is infeasible here. Torch backend exists (MLX is the Apple-optimised path).
methods.leakage_risk: HIGH (PDB + AFDB distillation covers the benchmark's pre-2023 depositions)
methods.orthogonality: Same ESM-2 conditioning as the project's distogram -> shared error source. The generative/ensemble head is the only novel part.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Low priority. If the 100M checkpoint turns out to condition on ESM-2 650M (already on disk), it is the ONLY end-to-end folder that could plausibly run here; a 20-sample ensemble per target could serve as an extra candidate donor into the K=500 pool. Verify the ESM dependency before spending time.

methods.name: PEP-FOLD3 / PEP-FOLD4
methods.predicts: de novo peptide structure from sequence, coarse-grained, pH-dependent force field
methods.training_data_cutoff: 27-state HMM structural alphabet learned from PDB (pre-2009); SVM SA-profile predictor over PSI-BLAST PSSMs
methods.short_length_performance: Best rigid-core conformations ~1.5 A from NMR (vs 1.7 A for PEP-FOLD1). Linear 25-36-mers: lowest-energy model 4.8 A (full structure) / 3.4 A (rigid core); 5 lowest-energy clusters average 3.6 / 2.8 A. In the APPTEST benchmark PEP-FOLD scored 2.05 A on 42 short (9-25 aa) peptides.
methods.source_of_number: NAR 2012 W288; NAR 2016 W449; Brief Bioinform 2021 bbab308 Table
methods.code_weights: web server + downloadable binaries; no permissive open-source licence
methods.cpu_feasible: YES (coarse-grained Monte Carlo, minutes on CPU), but licensing/packaging is the obstacle; the ALGORITHM is trivially reimplementable.
methods.leakage_risk: LOW (the SA alphabet is generic local geometry, not target structures)
methods.orthogonality: HIGH and this is the key entry in this table. PEP-FOLD's retrieval key is a per-position 27-state STRUCTURAL-ALPHABET PROFILE predicted from sequence; this project's key is a raw BLOSUM62 sum. Two different questions are being asked of the library.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Do not install PEP-FOLD; STEAL ITS KEY. Replace/augment the BLOSUM62 retrieval score with a per-position predicted torsion-state profile score. See lit_FINDINGS.md H1 - measured here to be worth 2.284 -> 1.64-1.70 A on FAIL18 pool-best under an oracle and under 20-30% biased noise.

methods.name: APPTEST
methods.predicts: inter-residue CA-CA / CB-CB distances AND phi/psi from sequence; then restrained simulated annealing in XPLOR-NIH / CYANA
methods.training_data_cutoff: 2,265 experimental peptide structures 5-40 aa from DBAASP/APD3/ADAM/DRAMP/PEPstrMOD/PEP-2D + RCSB, 90% identity cut, PDB snapshot June 2021
methods.short_length_performance: Short peptides 9-25 aa (n=42): APPTEST 1.96 A vs PEP-FOLD 2.05 A vs PEPstrMOD 4.66 A. Long 26-40 aa (n=30): 3.20 vs 3.43. Cyclic (n=34): 1.99 vs 2.71. Overall best model 1.9 A, native/near-native for 97% of 356 test peptides. Selection is by lowest XPLOR-NIH energy / CYANA target function (deployable, not oracle).
methods.code_weights: web server + compiled Linux binary; no source
methods.cpu_feasible: YES architecturally (small 1D-CNN + gated residual blocks; annealing in torsion space is cheap for n<=16). The published binary is Linux-only, but the architecture is ~200 lines.
methods.leakage_risk: HIGH if the binary is used (its training set is exactly the same short-peptide PDB universe as this benchmark); NONE if the ARCHITECTURE is reimplemented under this project's leave-fold-out discipline.
methods.orthogonality: MEDIUM-HIGH. APPTEST predicts the SAME quantity as the project's distogram (distances) but adds TORSIONS, and it folds from restraints instead of retrieving. The terminal operator is completely different: the project cannot produce a structure that is not a convex combination of retrieved windows; APPTEST has no retrieval bottleneck, which is exactly the FAIL18 defect (top-75 recall = 0).
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Two separable steals: (i) add a leave-fold-out per-residue phi/psi (or torsion-bin) head next to the existing distogram; (ii) add a restraint-driven fold-from-scratch arm (L-BFGS / simulated annealing over phi,psi minimising the distogram Bayes risk, multi-start) as a SECOND hypothesis generator whose output competes with the retrieval average. Falsifier: does the de-novo arm beat the retrieval arm on the 18 zero-recall targets?

methods.name: LassoPred
methods.predicts: 3D structure of lasso peptides: an ML annotator (ring/loop/tail lengths, isopeptide + plug classifiers) + a geometric constructor
methods.training_data_cutoff: 47 unique lasso peptide PDB structures, augmented to 905 dipeptide fragments; cutoff 2024-03-15
methods.short_length_performance: Top-3 ring/loop/tail annotation accuracy 0.92 on a 12-LaP blind test; mean CA-RMSD 3.2 +/- 1.0 A on correctly annotated structures, 3.0 +/- 1.3 A after 100 ns MD. AF2/ESMFold cannot produce the lariat topology at all; AF3 fails 10/12 on PDB LaPs and reaches 8% on the RODEO set.
methods.code_weights: GitHub, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (non-commercial, no derivatives - a real constraint)
methods.cpu_feasible: YES. <5 min on an RTX 2080 for the whole pipeline; the annotator is a small classifier and the constructor is geometry, so CPU cost is seconds-to-minutes.
methods.leakage_risk: HIGH for 3 of the 4 lasso targets in FAIL18: 2N5C (2015), 7JS6 (2020), 7LCW (2021) are inside the 47-structure training set with near-certainty. 9KAR (released 2025-04-16) is post-cutoff and is the only clean test.
methods.orthogonality: TOTAL. Encodes a topological constraint (threaded macrolactam, isopeptide Gly1/Cys1 to Asp8/9-Glu8/9) that neither BLOSUM retrieval nor a distogram over CA distances can express.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Class router: detect the lasso motif from sequence (position-1 G/C plus D/E at position 7-9 plus a RiPP-like composition), then emit a LassoPred/threaded-template structure instead of the retrieval average. Ceiling: 4 targets x (6.17 - 3.2) = -0.094 A on the 126 mean, -0.66 A on the FAIL18 mean. Report 9KAR separately as the only leakage-clean instance.

methods.name: CORDAX / WALTZ-DB 2.0 / ZipperDB (steric-zipper propensity)
methods.predicts: per-hexapeptide amyloid/steric-zipper propensity AND the predicted zipper topology (which of the 8 Eisenberg classes)
methods.training_data_cutoff: WALTZ-DB 2.0: 1,416 experimentally characterised hexapeptides (in-vitro aggregation assays, not PDB coordinates); the 2025 ML model is trained on ~4M ZipperDB Rosetta threading predictions
methods.short_length_performance: ML replication of the ZipperDB 3D-profile achieves ~93.5% classification overlap; CORDAX reports the correct zipper topology at high accuracy. No CA-RMSD numbers (it is a propensity classifier, not a structure predictor).
methods.code_weights: CORDAX web server; WALTZ-DB open database; the 2025 zipper-propensity model is open
methods.cpu_feasible: YES - hexapeptide scan of a 13-mer is 8 windows of a tiny classifier, microseconds. WALTZ-DB can be used to train a local LFO classifier from scratch with no external inference at all.
methods.leakage_risk: NONE for the propensity models (trained on aggregation ASSAYS, not on the deposited coordinates of these targets)
methods.orthogonality: TOTAL. Trained on in-vitro aggregation phenotypes. Nothing about BLOSUM similarity or an ESM distogram encodes 'this segment forms a cross-beta steric zipper and is therefore fully extended'.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Class router again: if the peptide is called a steric-zipper former, emit a near-ideal EXTENDED strand instead of the retrieval average. Measured locally (this agent): the fully extended template (phi=-180,psi=180) gives 0.27 / 0.43 / 0.65 / 0.72 / 1.23 / 2.41 A on 2BFI / 5W52 / 5V5B / 7VI4 / 7N2I / 3SGO, versus shipped 7.03 / 5.07 / 3.61 / 3.90 / 2.50 / 6.62. Worth -0.183 A on the 126 mean and -0.87 A on the FAIL18 mean if the detector is perfect.

methods.name: ALBATROSS (sparrow / idptools)
methods.predicts: sequence -> ensemble Rg, end-to-end distance Re, polymer scaling exponent nu, asphericity
methods.training_data_cutoff: trained on Mpipi-GG coarse-grained simulations of synthetic + natural IDR sequences; validated against SAXS. NO PDB coordinates in the training set.
methods.short_length_performance: R^2 = 0.994 against Mpipi-GG Re; strong correlation with SAXS Rg. Not benchmarked on structured peptides (its domain is IDRs), which is the main caveat.
methods.code_weights: open (idptools/sparrow), permissive; BRNN-LSTM, sub-million parameters
methods.cpu_feasible: YES - milliseconds per sequence, tens of MB.
methods.leakage_risk: NONE - it has never seen a PDB structure, let alone these.
methods.orthogonality: HIGH for the specific scalar the distogram gets wrong. Measured locally (this agent): the shipped distogram's normalised end-to-end distance has |true - predicted| correlating r = 0.531 with the shipped RMSD across all 126 targets; on the 12 worst targets the gap exceeds 0.25 and their mean shipped RMSD is 4.90 vs 3.30 for the rest. The distogram systematically UNDER-predicts extension (S7-2's compactness shift, made concrete).
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Use predicted Rg/Re/nu as a GLOBAL SCALE CONSTRAINT: (a) re-rank / re-weight the K=500 pool by agreement of each window's Rg with the predicted Rg; (b) add a global-dimension term to the projection objective. Caveat to test first: ALBATROSS assumes a disordered chain, so it may be systematically wrong for the helical majority. Falsifier: does predicted Rg correlate with the native Rg on the 126 at all (r > 0.4)? If not, kill it in one hour.

methods.name: metapredict V3
methods.predicts: per-residue disorder score and predicted AF2 pLDDT, from sequence only
methods.training_data_cutoff: disorder consensus + AFDB pLDDT distillation, 2024
methods.short_length_performance: Proteome-scale in seconds; V3 gives 5-10x CPU speedup over V2. No peptide-specific accuracy published.
methods.code_weights: open, permissive, pip-installable
methods.cpu_feasible: YES - BRNN-LSTM, milliseconds, tens of MB
methods.leakage_risk: LOW (pLDDT head is distilled from AFDB, which is UniProt-based predicted structure, not these PDB entries)
methods.orthogonality: MEDIUM. Gives a cheap 'is this peptide structured at all' gate, which is exactly the axis on which the coordinate-average operator is mis-specified (averaging 75 windows of a floppy peptide produces a collapsed non-peptide).
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Gate the terminal operator: for high-disorder targets, prefer a single medoid window over the 75-member coordinate average (the average has no meaning for an ensemble-averaged NMR peptide). Cheap A/B on the 126.

methods.name: Protein Blocks structural alphabet (de Brevern) + LOCUSTRA / PYTHIA / PBC5.0d predictors
methods.predicts: per-position 16-state local backbone conformation (5-residue windows) from sequence
methods.training_data_cutoff: PDB non-redundant sets; predictors variously 2008-2022
methods.short_length_performance: LOCUSTRA (2-layer SVM, 2008): Q16 = 61.0%, Q3 = 79.2% on 222 independent proteins. PBC5.0d reports Q16 ~80%. All trained on globular proteins; degradation on 9-16-mers is expected and unmeasured.
methods.source_of_number: J Chem Inf Model 2008 ci800178a; Comput Biol Chem 2022
methods.code_weights: several open implementations; the alphabet itself is public
methods.cpu_feasible: YES trivially
methods.leakage_risk: LOW-MEDIUM (trained on PDB local geometry; a leave-fold-out retrain on this project's own library removes it entirely)
methods.orthogonality: HIGH as a RETRIEVAL KEY (untested class per BRIEF S6-6). It asks 'which windows have the right local backbone shape', a question BLOSUM never asks.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: The central hypothesis H1. Train a leave-fold-out sequence(+ESM)->torsion-bin-posterior head on the project's own out-of-fold library, then retrieve K=500 by expected bin-match instead of BLOSUM sum. Measured requirement (this agent, lit_abego_noise.json): an oracle bin key takes FAIL18 pool-best from 2.284 to 1.640 and the near-native band count from 16/500 to 92/500; at 30% biased corruption it still gives 1.701; at 50% still 1.865; only a fully random key (2.533) is worse than BLOSUM. So a ~70%-accurate predictor suffices.

methods.name: Rosetta fragment picker (torsion_bin_probs / SS / profile scoring)
methods.predicts: n/a - it is the field's canonical fragment RETRIEVAL scorer
methods.training_data_cutoff: n/a
methods.short_length_performance: n/a; 15 years of Rosetta ab-initio results rest on it
methods.code_weights: Rosetta licence (free academic)
methods.cpu_feasible: YES (the scoring scheme, not the binary)
methods.leakage_risk: NONE
methods.orthogonality: This is the single clearest literature gap. The canonical fragment score is a WEIGHTED SUM of sequence-profile similarity + predicted secondary structure agreement + predicted torsion-bin probability agreement (the explicit torsion_bin_probs flag). This project uses only the first term, and in its weakest form (a raw BLOSUM62 sum rather than a PSSM profile score).
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Reimplement the multi-term fragment score with leave-fold-out learned weights. Component ablation on the 126 tells you which term carries the FAIL18 recall.

methods.name: Foldseek 3Di alphabet / ProstT5 (AA -> 3Di)
methods.predicts: 3Di: a 20-state alphabet describing each residue's geometry relative to its nearest TERTIARY neighbour; ProstT5 translates sequence -> 3Di without folding
methods.training_data_cutoff: ProstT5 = ProtT5-XL-U50 (3B params) fine-tuned on 17M AFDB structures
methods.short_length_performance: No short-peptide numbers. The Foldseek paper itself states 3Di's information density is HIGHEST in conserved cores and LOWEST in coils/loops - the exact opposite of a backbone alphabet.
methods.code_weights: Foldseek GPL-3.0; ProstT5 open on HuggingFace
methods.cpu_feasible: Foldseek YES; ProstT5 NO on this box (3B-parameter T5, ~12 GB fp32 / ~6 GB fp16 vs ~5 GB free). The CNN 3Di head on top of the encoder is cheap, but the encoder is not.
methods.leakage_risk: MEDIUM (AFDB-trained)
methods.orthogonality: REJECT ON PRINCIPLE, and this is a useful negative. A 9-16-residue peptide has almost no tertiary contacts, so 3Di collapses into its low-information coil states. The right structural alphabet for peptides is a BACKBONE alphabet (ABEGO / Protein Blocks / PEP-FOLD's 27-state SA), which is what H1 uses. Do not spend the sprint on 3Di.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: None. Documented here so the coordinator does not fund it.

methods.name: SaProt / ESM-3 (structure-token PLMs)
methods.predicts: joint sequence+structure representations over a 441-token structure-aware vocabulary
methods.training_data_cutoff: AFDB40 + PDB; SaProt 650M (ESM-2 architecture)
methods.short_length_performance: none published for peptides
methods.code_weights: SaProt open; ESM-3 open-weights small variant, licence-restricted
methods.cpu_feasible: SaProt 650M MARGINAL (~2.6 GB fp32, same as the ESM-2 650M already on disk); ESM-3 NO
methods.leakage_risk: HIGH (AFDB + PDB)
methods.orthogonality: LOW. SaProt REQUIRES a structure to tokenise; for the target we have none, so it can only score library windows - and it inherits both the 3Di degeneracy problem above and the ESM-2 error structure the project already has.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: None recommended.

methods.name: ProteinMPNN / ESM-IF (inverse folding as a scorer)
methods.predicts: p(sequence | backbone); used here as a nativeness score, not a designer
methods.training_data_cutoff: PDB <= 2020 (ProteinMPNN, ~1.7M chains at 30% identity); ESM-IF adds 12M AF2 predictions
methods.short_length_performance: Inverse-folding log-likelihoods correlate well with stability (ddG) and mutational fitness; no published peptide-scale MQA numbers. ProteinMPNN is ~1.7M parameters.
methods.code_weights: ProteinMPNN MIT, open; ESM-IF MIT
methods.cpu_feasible: YES for ProteinMPNN - 1.7M params, a 13-residue backbone scores in milliseconds on CPU; 500 candidates/target is seconds. This is the cheapest external model in the whole table.
methods.leakage_risk: LOW-MEDIUM. It has seen PDB backbones including some of these, but it is scoring SEQUENCE GIVEN BACKBONE, so it cannot memorise 'target X has structure Y' in a directly exploitable way. Still, report it as a learned-on-PDB component.
methods.orthogonality: HIGH for the in-band ranking problem. Every in-band ranker the project has tried (223 features, ridge/GBT/MLP) reads the distogram or window statistics. ProteinMPNN reads the BACKBONE GEOMETRY and asks a completely different question: 'would this sequence design this backbone?'. Its error mode (biased toward well-packed designable folds) is genuinely different from the distogram's (biased toward compactness).
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Score each of the K=500 windows (threaded with the TARGET sequence) by ProteinMPNN NLL, and use it as (i) a filter feature next to the distogram score and (ii) an in-band re-ranker. Falsifier: in-band Spearman on the 108 non-FAIL targets. Prior warning from the project record: 'nothing ranks within the pool' and fusion gains go as the square of the weaker channel's skill - so require in-band rho > 0.30 alone before believing any fusion. Also note ProteinMPNN's designability bias is exactly wrong for floppy/extended peptides, so expect it to help the 108 and hurt the FAIL18.

methods.name: TALOS-N (chemical shifts -> phi/psi)
methods.predicts: backbone phi/psi (and chi1 rotamers, and SS) from experimental NMR chemical shifts
methods.training_data_cutoff: ANN trained on shift/structure pairs; 2013
methods.short_length_performance: phi/psi predicted for >=90% of residues at ~12 degrees RMSD vs crystallographic values, error rate <3.5%. 12-degree torsion accuracy over a 13-mer implies roughly ~1 A CA-RMSD, i.e. it would essentially solve this benchmark where shifts exist.
methods.code_weights: free binary from the Bax lab (NIH); no source
methods.cpu_feasible: YES (seconds)
methods.leakage_risk: NOT leakage but a TASK CHANGE. Chemical shifts are experimental observables, not deposited coordinates - but they are the primary input from which the NMR structure was determined. Using them converts 'predict from sequence' into 'determine from NMR data'.
methods.orthogonality: TOTAL - it is an entirely different physical measurement channel.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Measured here: 79/126 targets (63%) and 10/18 FAIL18 have a linked BMRB entry with deposited shifts (s12/results/lit_bmrb_coverage.json). Recommended use is as a DIAGNOSTIC CEILING ARM, clearly labelled NMR-ASSISTED, not as a system component: it answers 'is the residual 3.2 A an information problem or an algorithm problem?' If a TALOS-N torsion prior takes the 79 shift-covered targets to ~1.5 A, the pipeline is information-limited and every reranking effort is misdirected. If it does not, the operator is the problem.

methods.name: CS-Rosetta
methods.predicts: de novo structure from chemical shifts, by shift-based fragment selection + Rosetta assembly
methods.training_data_cutoff: PDB fragment libraries
methods.short_length_performance: 0.7-1.8 A backbone RMSD on 16 proteins of 56-129 residues. Not validated at 9-16 residues (below its design regime).
methods.code_weights: free academic
methods.cpu_feasible: MARGINAL (Rosetta assembly is minutes-hours per target)
methods.leakage_risk: task change, as TALOS-N
methods.orthogonality: Same channel as TALOS-N; architecturally interesting because CS-Rosetta's contribution IS shift-based FRAGMENT SELECTION - i.e. the field's answer to 'what is the right retrieval key' when shifts exist is again a local-conformation key, not a sequence key.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Not a component. Cite as independent support for H1: both PEP-FOLD (sequence-only) and CS-Rosetta (shift-based) pick fragments by predicted local conformation.

methods.name: AF2 MSA-subsampling ensembles / AFsample2 / peptide conformational ensembles
methods.predicts: conformational ensembles rather than one structure
methods.training_data_cutoff: AF2 weights (PDB <= 2018)
methods.short_length_performance: 80-structure ensembles per peptide over 557 peptides: overall RMSD under 2.5 A and RMSF differences under 1.5 A (authors' summary).
methods.code_weights: open protocols on top of ColabFold
methods.cpu_feasible: NO (needs AF2, x80 samples)
methods.leakage_risk: HIGH
methods.orthogonality: Conceptually important: for a 13-mer with no MSA, MSA subsampling has nothing to subsample. The ensemble idea is the transferable part, and this project ALREADY has a 500-member ensemble - it simply collapses it with a coordinate average.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: The transferable lesson is about the TERMINAL OPERATOR, not the model. The natives are NMR ensemble representatives; scoring a single averaged structure against model 1 of a 20-model ensemble is partly a metric artefact. Cheap diagnostic: score against the full deposited ensemble (best-of-models, and ensemble-average) rather than model 1, and report how much of the 3.2 A is ensemble spread. This is close to free and has never been done in the record.

methods.name: BioEmu
methods.predicts: equilibrium conformational ensembles from sequence (AF2 evoformer trunk + denoising diffusion)
methods.training_data_cutoff: >200 ms of MD + PDB statics + experimental stabilities
methods.short_length_performance: none published for 9-16-mers; the model is aimed at folded domains and folding free energies
methods.code_weights: open (MIT-ish) on HuggingFace/GitHub
methods.cpu_feasible: NO - requires the AF2 evoformer (~3.5 GB of weights auto-downloaded) plus 30-50 diffusion steps x thousands of samples; single-GPU design.
methods.leakage_risk: HIGH (AF2 trunk)
methods.orthogonality: HIGH in principle (MD-derived, so it knows about flexibility rather than about crystal-like single states) but unreachable on this hardware.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Out of scope for this box. Note for the coordinator only if GPU time ever becomes available.

methods.name: PepFlow / PPFlow / PepGLAD / THFlow (peptide generative design)
methods.predicts: full-atom peptide BINDERS conditioned on a receptor structure
methods.training_data_cutoff: PepBDB / protein-peptide complexes
methods.short_length_performance: reported as design metrics (affinity, stability, diversity), never as RMSD-to-native for an isolated peptide
methods.code_weights: open
methods.cpu_feasible: NO (SE(3) flow matching, GPU)
methods.leakage_risk: n/a
methods.orthogonality: MISMATCHED TASK. Every one of these is receptor-conditioned design. None predicts the solution conformation of a free peptide. The apparent 2025 boom in 'peptide generative models' does not touch this project's problem - a useful negative for the coordinator.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: None.

methods.name: RFdiffusion / Genie2 / FrameFlow / Chroma (backbone generative models)
methods.predicts: unconditional or motif-scaffolded designable backbones
methods.training_data_cutoff: PDB; Genie2 trained with max length 256
methods.short_length_performance: Genie2 is strongest at short lengths, but 'designability' is measured by ProteinMPNN + AF2 self-consistency, not by agreement with any real peptide's solution structure.
methods.code_weights: open
methods.cpu_feasible: NO
methods.leakage_risk: n/a
methods.orthogonality: Actively WRONG-signed: these models are trained to produce IDEALISED, DESIGNABLE, well-packed backbones. This benchmark's hard cases are floppy, extended, membrane-bound and topologically exotic - the exact opposite of the designability prior.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: None. Explicitly deprioritise.

methods.name: MDGen
methods.predicts: generative MD trajectories (forward simulation, interpolation, inpainting)
methods.training_data_cutoff: MD of tetrapeptides
methods.short_length_performance: Transferable evaluation is on TETRAPEPTIDES only.
methods.code_weights: open
methods.cpu_feasible: NO (GPU-seconds quoted; and the length regime is wrong anyway)
methods.leakage_risk: NONE
methods.orthogonality: n/a - length mismatch is disqualifying (4 residues vs 9-16).
methods.wiring_hypothesis: None.

methods.name: UCBShift 2.0 / SPARTA+ / ShiftX2 (forward chemical-shift prediction)
methods.predicts: chemical shifts GIVEN a structure
methods.training_data_cutoff: SPARTA+/SHIFTX+ sets consolidated, enriched from BMRB
methods.short_length_performance: RMSE 0.31 ppm (HN), 0.19 (Ha), 0.84 (C'), 0.81 (Ca), 1.00 (Cb), 1.81 (N) - on proteins, not peptides
methods.code_weights: open (UCBShift)
methods.cpu_feasible: YES (random-forest module)
methods.leakage_risk: UCBShift's transfer module explicitly looks up structural homologs with assigned shifts - that is a direct memorisation path for these very targets. Use only the ML module, never the transfer module.
methods.orthogonality: This is the RERANKER form of the NMR channel: for the 79 shift-covered targets, score each of the K=500 candidates by agreement between its predicted shifts and the deposited shifts. It is a completely external, physics-grounded discriminator - the first candidate in the whole record with a plausible route past the in-band ranking ceiling.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: NMR-ASSISTED ARM ONLY, clearly labelled. Diagnostic value: if shift-agreement reranking of the top-75 does not beat the distogram in-band, then the in-band problem is not about the strength of the ranker but about the pool.

methods.name: NetSurfP-3.0 / S4PRED / Porter 6 (secondary structure)
methods.predicts: Q3/Q8 secondary structure, RSA, disorder, phi/psi (NetSurfP-3.0 also outputs dihedrals)
methods.training_data_cutoff: PDB-derived training sets; standard practice EXCLUDES chains shorter than 20-30 residues
methods.short_length_performance: Porter 6 on a 2024 test set: Q3 84.56%, Q8 74.18% - on PROTEINS. NetSurfP-3.0 matches NetSurfP-2.0 at ~100x the speed using PLM embeddings. S4PRED is the single-sequence SOTA. Critically, the standard training protocol removes chains below ~20 residues, so accuracy on 9-16-mers is unmeasured and likely materially worse.
methods.code_weights: NetSurfP-3.0 open; S4PRED GPL
methods.cpu_feasible: YES (S4PRED is a small BiLSTM; NetSurfP-3.0 needs an ESM-1b/ProtT5 embedding, but ESM-2 650M is already on disk)
methods.leakage_risk: MEDIUM (PDB-trained; a leave-fold-out local retrain removes it)
methods.orthogonality: The SS content itself is only partly orthogonal (the distogram implicitly encodes helicity). But as a RETRIEVAL KEY it is untested (BRIEF S6-6 only tested it as an oracle FILTER, worth 0.21 A). The measurements in lit_FINDINGS.md show filter and key are entirely different levers.
methods.wiring_hypothesis: Feed H1: the torsion-bin head should be trained on the project's own out-of-fold windows using the ESM-2 features already banked, NOT imported from a protein-trained predictor - because these targets (designed, membrane, amyloid, lasso) are exactly where a globular-protein SS predictor breaks.
